title: What makes your blood type A, B, AB or O

figure.name: x-compare
figure.verdict: AB has both markers; O has neither

explain.say: Your blood type depends on tiny markers, called antigens, on the surface of your red blood cells. The two main markers are called A and B, and you inherit which ones you have from your parents.

explain.say: Type A blood has A markers on its red cells. Its plasma carries antibodies that attack B markers, so if type B cells get in, they clump together.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: AB has both markers; O has neither

explain.say: Type B blood is the mirror image: B markers on the cells and antibodies against A in the plasma.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: AB has both markers; O has neither

explain.say: Type AB has both markers and no antibodies against either. Type O has no A or B markers, so its red cells are not attacked by anyone's A or B antibodies, which is why O negative donors can give to almost anyone.

draw.name: x-compare
draw.verdict: AB has both markers; O has neither

faq.a: Your genes, from your parents, decide which markers your red blood cells carry. Having A markers makes you type A, B markers type B, both makes AB, and neither makes O.
Plasma contains antibodies against the markers your own cells lack. If blood with those markers is given, the antibodies make the donated cells clump and break up, so blood types must be matched.
Type O red cells have neither A nor B markers. Because there is nothing for A or B antibodies to attack, O negative red cells can be given to people of almost any type in an emergency.
asks: Why is O the universal donor?

faq.q: What does positive or negative mean in blood types?
faq.a: It refers to another marker called the Rh factor, or RhD. If your red cells have it you are positive, such as A positive; if not, you are negative.

faq.q: What is the most common blood type?
faq.a: It varies around the world, but types O and A are the most common overall, and AB is the rarest.

facts: The ABO blood groups were discovered by Karl Landsteiner in 1901.
Type AB red cells carry both A and B antigens; type O carries neither.
